state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's imagine a group of friends who all have different amounts of money. If everyone's amount of money is doubled or halved, would the difference in the amounts they have change? Think about how this relates to the heights of the plants in the scenario you provided.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I see what you mean... if everyone's money is doubled, like if one person has £10 and another has £20, the difference is still £10, so it stays the same? But wait, does that mean Katie is also right then, because adding 3 cm to each plant would also keep the difference the same?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it in terms of a group of friends who all have different heights. If everyone's height is increased by the same amount, would the difference in height between them change? Think about how this relates to adding 3 cm to each plant in the scenario.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, yeah! If everyone grows by 3 cm, like if one friend is 150 cm and another is 160 cm, they're still 10 cm apart... so the difference stays the same. So that means both Tom and Katie are right then? I'm confused now because I thought only Tom was right before.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies to prompt reasoning but fails to address the mathematical error in the student's logic (doubling does change the range), leading the student to an incorrect conclusion that both Tom and Katie are right when only Katie is correct.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (friends with money, friends with different heights) to help the student understand the abstract mathematical concept of range, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
